claims.text: Introducing a Ti-rich secondary phase into an fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti matrix will raise coercivity above 100 Oe.
The Ti-rich secondary phase will enhance coercivity by providing magnetic domain-wall pinning sites.
Interfacial exchange coupling between the fcc matrix and Ti-rich phase will alter the local magnetic ground state.
The Ti-rich secondary phase can be introduced without disrupting the stability of the fcc matrix.
The Ti-rich phase will be non-magnetic or weakly magnetic.
A Ti-rich barrier will suppress orbital-moment quenching in adjacent fcc matrix regions.
Suppression of orbital-moment quenching near the precipitates will increase magnetic anisotropy.
The initial single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti alloy has coercivity below 10 Oe.
Low coercivity in the initial alloy is caused by suppressed orbital moments and weak magnetic anisotropy.
Adding Ti beyond its solid-solubility limit and heat treating the alloy will precipitate a Ti-rich secondary phase such as C14 Laves.
The fcc matrix will remain stable and the Ti-rich secondary phase will not dissolve over 300–600 K.
The intervention will produce nanoscale-to-microscale Ti-rich precipitates with coherent or semi-coherent interfaces in the fcc matrix.
Ti-rich precipitates will introduce local strain fields and modify electronic structure at fcc/precipitate interfaces.
Domain walls will require a higher external field to overcome the interfacial pinning-energy barrier.
The dual-phase alloy will have moderately lower saturation magnetization than the single-phase alloy.
The magnetic ordering temperature of the dual-phase alloy will remain above room temperature.
Ti concentrations of 5–15 at.% define a viable range for precipitation strengthening without loss of the fcc matrix.
Excessive Ti may cause brittle-phase formation or complete transformation to non-fcc structures.
